tip: Trotzdem is an adverb filling slot 1, so the verb comes next and the subject follows: Trotzdem gebe ich. The preposition trotz instead needs a noun after it.
The receiver takes dative with no word for to: dem Gast means to the guest. German marks it with the article, not with a preposition.
The stray vor at the end belongs to vorlesen (read aloud): it splits off from lese and parks at the clause end. Without it, lesen just means read.
With no article, the adjective carries the gender signal itself: frisches Obst uses the -es ending to flag that Obst is a das-word.
Guter Rat ist teuer is a set proverb, said when you are stuck and a good solution is hard to find. Literally it is good advice is expensive.
German waits on, not for: warten auf, so wartet auf seine Mutter is literally waits on his mother where English says waits for.
Plural die forces the -en ending on the adjective: die kleinen Kinder. It stays -en for every adjective after a plural die.
After das, the adjective needs only a light -e ending: das kleine Kind. The article already shows the gender, so the adjective stays simple.
Start with Danach and the verb still holds slot 2, so the subject drops in behind it: Danach räumen wir, not Danach wir räumen.
After einen the adjective takes -en: einen großen Hund. English leaves big unchanged, but German bends the adjective to match.
In the perfect tense hat holds slot 2 and the participle waits at the very end: hat einen langen Brief an ihre Freundin geschrieben.
The verb stays second no matter what comes first: front Am meisten and vermisse still lands in slot 2, pushing ich behind it.
noch nie means never once up to now, stronger than a plain nie: hat sich noch nie ... beschwert says it has simply never happened.
German builds the most-often adverb as am plus -sten: Am häufigsten means most frequently. There is no separate word like most.
The stray an at the end belongs to anrufen (to phone): ruft seinen Bruder ... an. On its own, ruft just means calls out or shouts.
Könntest du is the polite could you, softer than the blunt Kannst du (can you). It turns a demand into a courteous request.
After the dative dem, the adjective flattens to -en: dem alten Patienten. The strong dem already carries the case, so alt just takes -en.
dem Briefträger marks the receiver as dative: the to of to the mail carrier lives inside the article dem, not in word order or a preposition.
The modal Können pairs with an infinitive parked at the very end: Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen. In a yes/no question the modal leads and sprechen closes the clause.
English drops the to, but German marks it with dative: dem Mann etwas Geld means some money to the man, shown by dem, not a preposition.
helfen takes a dative object, so it is helfe meinem Vater, not den Vater. English treats help as a direct-object verb, but German does not.
darfst ... nicht means must not, a ban: darfst ... nicht rauchen is smoking is forbidden. Do not mix it with muss nicht, which means need not.
möchte is the polite would like, softer than the blunt will (want): möchte eine Tasse Tee is a courteous way to order.
Ihm wurde ... geschenkt is literally to him was gifted. German keeps the receiver in dative, Ihm, where English promotes it to he was given.
weil sends its verb to the very end: weil die Sonne blendet puts blendet last. Everything after weil reorders around that final verb.
Dürfte ich is an extra-polite may I, one notch softer than darf ich: Dürfte ich bitte die Speisekarte sehen is the gentlest way to ask.
The recipient takes the dative pronoun dir, not dich: Ich bringe dir means I bring to you. dich would be the accusative object instead.
Verbs with an inseparable prefix skip the usual ge- in the participle: haben uns entschlossen (decided), never geentschlossen.
German parks the participle at the clause end: hat seine Meinung über das Thema geändert. English keeps changed right after has, but German waits.
aus splits off to the end and means off here: mache das Licht ... aus is turn the light off. The base machen alone just means make or do.
helfen acts on a dative object: hilft dem Patienten, not den Patienten. A few verbs like danken behave the same way.
in dem means in which: after a preposition the relative word takes its case, and neuter das Hotel becomes dem in the dative.
zum is zu dem fused into one word: zu always takes dative, so zum Kurs means to the course, and zur Arbeit does the same for feminine.
fehlen flips the English miss: Sie fehlt ihren Eltern means she is missing to her parents. The missed person is the subject, the missers go dative.
möchte is a fixed polite I would like: Ich möchte mich bei Ihnen bedanken softens the request. Use it whenever English says I would like.
The der in nach der Reise is feminine, not masculine: die Reise shifts to der in the dative, which nach always triggers.
The prefix decides the ge-: separable ein- keeps it in eingesehen, but inseparable ent- drops it in entschuldigt, never geentschuldigt.
eines Geschenks is genitive because anstatt demands it, not because of possession: anstatt, wegen and trotz all force the genitive.
darf ... nicht means must not, a prohibition: darf das Gebäude ... nicht betreten is entering is forbidden. muss nicht instead means need not.
ob means whether and pushes its verb to the end: ob das Restaurant heute geöffnet hat lands hat at the close of the clause.
zwischen takes dative for a fixed location: zwischen der Post und dem Rathaus marks where something sits. Motion toward would switch it to accusative.
hinter takes dative for a standing-still position: steht hinter dem Zaun. Moving to behind the fence would flip it to accusative, den Zaun.
dem Kellner means to the waiter with no separate word for to: the receiver of geben goes dative, and dem carries that to inside it.
The modal könnt sits in slot 2 and sends its partner verb to the end: Ihr könnt das Fahrrad gerne ausleihen. The infinitive ausleihen closes the clause.
German reverses the miss: Das Spielzeug fehlt dem kleinen Mädchen means the toy is missing to the girl, where English says the girl misses the toy.
English believes the salesman as a direct object, but German gives the person dative: Ich glaube dem Verkäufer, not den Verkäufer.
